newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Killer brain disease may be passed on by blood-WHO.
newsitem.headline: Killer brain disease may be passed on by blood-WHO.

text.p: The World Health Organisation has declared that the human form of mad cow disease, a fatal brain disorder, can be passed on by blood transfusions and certain groups of people at risk must not donate blood.

The frightening findings were presented to the United Nations health agency by a leading U.S. scientist who identified three high-risk donor categories after his experiments with mice showed blood plasma could transmit the disease agent.

The WHO endorsed the findings on Wednesday after a two-day consultation with a group of 50 international medical experts on Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) and bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), which causes mad cow disease.

The experts' recommendations will now be sent to the 191 member states of WHO, which is co-ordinating world-wide surveillance amid fears that mad cow disease can cross over to humans in a new form of the brain-wasting CJD.

Paul Brown, a leading expert on both CJD and BSE based at the National Institute of Health in Bethesda, Maryland, said he injected blood from mice infected with the human form of mad cow disease into the brains of healthy mice, which became ill.
He told a final news conference that the risk of blood plasma passing on CJD was small, but still existed.

This would also apply to the "new variant" of CJD, v-CJD, thought to be derived from the agent which causes mad cow disease that takes its name from the behaviour of infected cows which go mad, twitch and kick in a frenzy until they die.
Brown identified three high-risk groups which he said should not be allowed to donate blood. These were:

- people who received growth hormones in the early 1980s. A proportion of these people have already died from CJD because they received contaminated growth hormones and deaths are continuing, Brown said.

- people who received a transplant of a human brain tissue called dura mater -- the outermost and toughest covering of the brain used in Neurosurgery to patch damaged membranes of patients and extracted from corpses that died from CJD.
- members of families affected with the disease or families bearing known mutations that could cause CJD. This group was thought to be genetically more likely to contract the disease.
"Members of such families should not donate blood because a certain number of them are going to die from CJD," Brown said.
"These groups should be excluded from donating blood."
He said dura mater was still being used in Neurosurgery and other operations such as replacement of eardrums and intestinal surgery and in gall bladder and that this had to be stopped.

"In view of transmissions of CJD using this substance, and view of the possibility of using alternative materials, the working group recommended that this material dura mater should not be used for any purpose in the future," he said.
The mad cow disease is caused by so-called prions or infectious proteins that are not destroyed by cooking, canning or freezing and can survive in the soil for years according to scientists.

Some experts have long suspected that these proteins, which could concentrate in the brain and nervous tissue, where they lead to holes that give the brain a spongy appearance like Swiss cheese, could be transmitted in the blood.

CJD is a painful degenerative disease which gives an infected patient involuntary spasms that then deteriorate into blindness and epilepsy. As it progresses, the prions slowly work themselves into the brain tissues.
There is no known treatment or cure for BSE in bovines or CJD in humans.
